nameStory: The "fleabane" name comes from an old belief that burning these plants would repel fleas - though there's little evidence this actually worked! The "marsh" part is spot-on, as this plant loves wet, salty places. Some folks also call it "sweetscent" or "shrubby camphorweed" for its distinctive fragrance.
description: Marsh fleabane is a sturdy, shrub-like wildflower that grows 2-4 feet tall in salty wetlands. It has thick, fleshy leaves and clusters of small pink-purple flowers that lack the white petals typical of many asters. The whole plant has a strong, camphor-like smell that you'll notice before you even touch it. Despite being in the sunflower family, it looks quite different from typical daisies.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small pink-purple flower heads in dense, flat-topped clusters, lacking the white ray petals of typical asters - just tiny tubular flowers packed together

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Thick, fleshy, oval leaves with toothed edges that feel succulent-like and slightly sticky when crushed, arranged alternately on the stem

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Bushy, shrub-like plant 2-4 feet tall with multiple sturdy stems branching from the base, much more robust than typical wildflowers

idTips.label: Scent
idTips.description: Strong camphor or medicinal smell that's noticeable from several feet away, especially on warm days or when leaves are bruised

habitat: Found in salt marshes, tidal flats, and brackish wetlands along the New England coast. Thrives in salty soils that kill most other plants, often growing alongside salt marsh asters and sea lavender. Most common from southern Maine down to Connecticut's shoreline areas.

seasonality.spring: New shoots emerge as thick, fleshy stems with young leaves that already carry the distinctive camphor scent.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming period with dense clusters of pink-purple flowers attracting butterflies and other pollinators through late summer.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade to fluffy seed heads, and leaves may take on purplish tints while retaining their succulent texture.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to ground level, leaving dried stems and seed heads that persist into early winter.

funFact: This plant is like a natural salt filter - it can actually absorb salt from seawater through its roots and concentrate it in special cells in its leaves, allowing it to thrive where the salt would kill almost any other flowering plant!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with salt marsh asters, but marsh fleabane lacks the white daisy-like petals and has much thicker, fleshier leaves. Remember: if it smells like medicine and has no white petals, it's probably fleabane!
contextualKnowledge: Despite the name "fleabane," this plant is unrelated to true fleabanes (Erigeron species) and doesn't actually repel fleas. The common names can be confusing since several unrelated plants share the "fleabane" name due to old folk beliefs about their pest-repelling properties.
compareHints: Marsh fleabane is the only Pluchea species commonly found in New England. Compared to other members of the aster family, it's unusually shrubby and salt-tolerant, with much fleshier leaves and flowers that lack the typical daisy appearance. Its camphor scent and succulent-like leaves make it quite distinctive among New England's coastal wildflowers.
